questions.q: Why can engineered features like raw price levels or rolling-sum volume indicators be non-stationary, even after Chapter 1 already converted prices to returns?
options: Because any feature built from a levels-tracking or cumulative quantity (a price level, a cumulative fundamental, a rolling sum riding a drifting regime) inherits the same trending-mean or trending-variance behavior that raw prices had
Because pandas rolling functions always introduce non-stationarity
Because stationarity only applies to the original price series, never to derived features
Because non-stationarity only affects fundamental data, never technical features
questions.explain: Stationarity problems aren't unique to raw prices -- any feature built by tracking a level or summing over a window that rides a drifting regime (like the volume example, which rides a liquidity-regime drift) can fail the constant-mean/constant-variance definition just as badly.

questions.q: In the worked example, what happened to the ADF test results after applying a 60-day rolling z-score to the raw price level and the rolling-sum volume feature?
options: Both results stayed exactly the same as before the transform
Both features went from failing to reject the unit-root null (p = 0.3555 and p = 0.8849) to rejecting it decisively (p = 0.0052 and p < 0.0001)
The ADF test cannot be run on z-scored data
Only the volume feature became stationary; the price level stayed non-stationary
questions.explain: Before the transform, both features failed to reject the non-stationarity null. After the 60-day rolling z-score, both rejected the null decisively, confirming the transform fixed the non-stationarity.

questions.q: Why did the 'global z-score' version of the price level produce the exact same ADF statistic and p-value as the untransformed raw price level?
options: Because a global z-score is a fixed linear rescaling of the whole series -- it shifts and stretches the data once but does not remove a trend, so it cannot fix non-stationarity
Because the ADF test ignores z-scored data entirely
Because the global z-score was computed incorrectly
Because global z-scores always produce stationary output on other datasets
questions.explain: A global z-score (subtracting one full-sample mean and dividing by one full-sample standard deviation) is just an affine transform, which leaves the series' trend and unit root intact -- unlike a rolling z-score, which re-centers using only a trailing window.

questions.q: What is the main problem with using a single global z-score (computed over the entire dataset, including future observations) to normalize a financial feature?
options: It runs too slowly compared to a rolling z-score
It uses information from the future relative to any earlier point in the sample, and it assumes the feature's distribution is stable across the whole sample even through regime changes
It can only be applied to fundamental data, not price data
It always produces values outside the range -1 to 1
questions.explain: A global z-score leaks future distributional information into feature values computed at earlier points in time, and it assumes a single stable mean/variance across the whole sample -- an assumption that breaks down across a genuine regime change.

questions.q: Why are rank or percentile transforms described as 'stationary by construction' and useful in cross-sectional equity factor work?
options: Because a rank is always bounded (e.g., between 0 and 1) regardless of how the underlying raw values drift, and one extreme value only shifts a rank by one position rather than distorting a mean or standard deviation
Because ranks are always equal to the raw value divided by two
Because rank transforms eliminate the need for any ADF testing on any feature
Because ranks cannot be computed on financial data
questions.explain: A rank or percentile is bounded by definition no matter how the underlying raw values drift over time, and it is robust to outliers since an extreme value only changes its own rank position rather than distorting a mean/std used by the whole series.
